analysis.one_liner: Allows pharmacists and wholesalers to import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and died at the end of the 108th Congress with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal drug law so licensed American pharmacists and wholesalers could import prescription drugs from Canada, where the same medicines often sell for much less. It would require registered Canadian sellers, lab testing for authenticity, detailed records of each shipment, and suspension of imports if counterfeit drugs showed up. It would also direct the government to leave alone individuals who bring in a personal 90-day supply from a licensed Canadian pharmacy with a valid prescription.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially seniors and people on long-term medications, would gain a legal, tested channel to buy the same drugs at Canadian prices. Community pharmacists and wholesalers could also compete by sourcing from Canada.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write regulations letting licensed U.S. pharmacists and wholesalers import prescription drugs from Canada [S2][S3].

Requires that imported drugs be FDA-approved, tested at qualified U.S. laboratories for authenticity and degradation, tracked with lot numbers and shipment documentation, and subject to immediate suspension if counterfeits are found [S3].

Mandates a waiver allowing individuals to import up to a 90-day personal supply from a licensed, registered Canadian pharmacy with a valid prescription, and directs enforcement to focus only on imports posing a real public health threat [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. prices would face competition from lower Canadian prices, would bear the cost. The government would also cover the cost of regulating and monitoring imports.

drawbacks.text: Safety risk is the central objection: even with lab testing and registration requirements, an open importation channel increases the chance that counterfeit, mishandled, or degraded drugs reach patients, and critics argued FDA oversight could not fully police a foreign supply chain [S2][S3].

The bill carries real compliance costs for pharmacists and wholesalers — batch testing, documentation of every shipment, and foreign-seller registration — which could limit how much of the price savings actually reaches consumers [S3].
Health officials have long argued importation mainly relieves pressure for domestic price reform, since Canada's supply could not cover U.S. demand without straining Canada's own drug system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers genuine savings to consumers with unusually detailed safety machinery — lab testing, lot tracking, registration, and suspension powers — so its design is more careful than most importation proposals. The honest tradeoff is that no amount of paperwork fully eliminates the risk of counterfeit drugs entering through a new channel, and the costs of that machinery fall on the small pharmacies and wholesalers who would do the importing. Whether patients would see large savings depends on how much of the Canadian discount survived those compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Health Subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Wexler introduced the bill on January 20, 2004, as the sole sponsor, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on January 20, 2004 [S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health on February 3, 2004, and no further action was taken; the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers were better off: the bill that would have opened a lower-priced Canadian supply channel never advanced, leaving U.S. drug prices — and the industry's price structure — untouched.

for.name: Rep. Robert Wexler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it carried no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in the Health Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have consistently opposed prescription drug importation measures in Congress, lobbying against bills that would open a Canadian price channel.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no party breakdown exists; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and sat in a committee controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: Importation would expose their U.S. prices to competition from lower Canadian prices on the same FDA-approved drugs. Every prior importation bill in this era faced the industry's full lobbying weight, and this one died without ever reaching a vote.

The bill's importers are licensed U.S. pharmacists and wholesalers, giving them a new lower-cost supply channel, though it comes with testing, recordkeeping, and registration burdens they would have to pay for.
The bill requires authenticity and degradation testing at Secretary-approved 'qualified laboratories' in the United States, creating paying work for that industry.
